## Highlights

### Hand a command the terminal

Some commands only work on a real terminal: `gh auth login`, `aws sso login`,
`gcloud auth login`, `docker login`. They prompt, open a browser and print a
code, and until now coda ran every tool without a TTY — so those commands
either failed immediately or blocked until a timeout.

The agent can now hand the terminal over. Coda suspends, the command owns the
screen, and when it exits coda redraws and reports the status:

```
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  terminal handed to: gh auth login
  coda is suspended. Finish there, or press Ctrl+C to abort.
──────────────────────────────────────────────────

… the command’s own output …

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  back in coda -- gh auth login exited 0
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

- **Approved before it runs, every time.** There is no list of permitted
  commands to keep current: an allowlist would need a release for each new tool,
  and an entry approved once could be re-run later without asking.
- **Exit status only reaches the model.** The command writes to the screen, so
  coda never captures it — and a login prints a URL and sometimes a one-time
  code, which should not enter a transcript that is saved and re-sent as
  history.
- **`Ctrl+C` stops the command, not coda.**
- **Exclusive.** Refused while another session is mid-turn, because that
  session's repaint would draw over the prompt.
- **No credentials in the command.** A stored secret, or a `{{secret:NAME}}`
  placeholder, is refused: substitution and output redaction belong to
  `use_secret`, whose output *is* captured.

### `!command` runs in the shell

A line starting with `!` runs in a shell instead of going to the agent:

```
!git status
!npm test 2>&1 | tail -20
!terminal gh auth login
```

- **No approval and no model round trip.** It is not sent to the agent and
  costs no tokens.
- **Output is redacted**, including the echoed command line, so a command that
  prints a stored credential shows `[redacted]`. The consequence is that
  `!curl -u user:token …` hides what was typed — the price of never writing it
  to disk.
- **When a command needs a terminal**, coda does not guess from its name. It
  runs the command and offers the handover in two situations: it exited at once
  with no output and a failure, or it is still running and has produced nothing
  for a few seconds. The second uses a silence timer reset by any output, so a
  command that keeps talking is never interrupted however long it runs.
  `!terminal <command>` goes straight there.

### Token usage is recorded

Every assistant reply now records what the provider reported it cost:

```json
"usage": {
  "promptTokens": 1656,
  "completionTokens": 1,
  "totalTokens": 1657,
  "details": { "prompt_cache_hit_tokens": 1408, "prompt_cache_miss_tokens": 248 },
  "model": "deepseek-flash"
}
```

Counts and the model name only — never message text. `unknown: true` marks a
turn whose provider reported nothing, which is distinct from a turn that used
nothing: not every provider honours the request for usage. A turn can make
several requests (one per tool round-trip); the numbers are sums and `unknown`
is sticky, so a partial total never reads as complete. Sessions written before
this have no `usage`, which a reader should treat as "not recorded".

### Credentials can be passed in the environment

`use_secret` gained `env`, for programs that read a credential from the
environment rather than stdin (`gh`, `curl -u`, anything using `$TOKEN`):

```jsonc
{ "command": ["gh", "pr", "create", "--fill"],
  "env": { "GH_TOKEN": "{{secret:github-token}}" } }
```

The value is merged over the inherited environment and passed with
`shell: false`, so `$` and backticks in a credential stay literal. A literal
secret in an env value is refused, as in `argv`. The approval prompt names the
variables: `(sets GH_TOKEN in its environment)`.

## Fixes

- **A model is offered only for the endpoint that serves it.** Selecting a
  vision-only model from the text column used to make the next message fail
  with `400 The supported API model names are …`.
- **Image support is taken from the endpoint where it is declared.** Providers
  that report capabilities in `GET /models` — `input_modalities`, or a
  prompt-image price — are believed over a hardcoded list of model names, which
  could not keep up with new providers. Endpoints that report nothing fall back
  to that list, unchanged.
- **Rate limits are waited out and explained.** A `429` is usually a per-minute
  rate limit, not a billing problem, but the retry backoff could not outlast a
  one-minute window and the message said only `429`. The delay now comes from
  the provider (`Retry-After`, the rate-limit reset headers, or the “retry in
  30.5s” in its own message), falling back to 1s → 4s → 10s, capped at 30s so a
  turn cannot appear to hang.
- **Provider error messages survive the SDK.** Google’s OpenAI-compatible
  endpoint returns errors as a JSON array, which the SDK cannot parse, so it
  discards the body and reports `429 status code (no body)`. The raw body is now
  read before that happens, so the provider’s explanation reaches the user.
- **New sessions can hand over the terminal.** A session’s first message takes
  a different path through the app, and only the other path was wired — so
  `gh auth login` as an opening message was refused after approval.
- **The image cursor is visible on the highlighted row**, where reverse video
  had been swallowing it.

## Known limitations

- **No browser opener of coda’s own.** On WSL, a login command that cannot
  launch a Windows browser will not have one launched for it. `gh` handles its
  own; a tool that does not will print a URL to open manually.
- **Long-running commands** (`npm run dev`) cannot be handed the terminal: the
  handover waits for the command to exit, so there is no way to report that it
  is running and return control.
- **`←/→ image` in `/model` operates on the default endpoint’s models.** A
  session switched to another endpoint refuses images rather than using that
  endpoint’s own vision models; scoping the image route per endpoint is not yet
  implemented.
